title: Postgres read replica lag causing slow queries
symptoms: Read queries returning stale data, replica lag ~30s, slower reads, DB alerts firing.
logs:
[WARNING] Replication lag on replica-3 exceeded threshold: 30s
[ERROR] Read query timeout on replica-3 after 8500ms
[WARNING] WAL sender on primary showing high pending bytes: 2.3GB
recent_change: Write throughput increased ~3x after a batch import feature deployed two hours ago.

analysis.summary: The database cluster is experiencing a 30‑second replication lag on replica‑3 after a recent batch import that tripled write throughput. The lag is causing stale reads and slow query timeouts.

likely_causes.cause: WAL backlog due to 3x write throughput from the new batch import
likely_causes.reasoning: Logs show 2.3 GB pending WAL bytes and the incident matches TEST‑001 where the same pattern was observed.
pg_stat_replication indicated elevated write_lag and flush_lag, and the replica was identified as I/O bound in TEST‑001.
Resolution of TEST‑001 increased replica IOPS from 3000 to 6000, implying the original IOPS were a limiting factor.

relevant_past_incidents.relevance: Same service, same symptoms, identical replication lag and write spike
relevant_past_incidents.previous_resolution: Throttled batch import to 500 rows/s, increased replica IOPS from 3000 to 6000, enabled WAL compression, and added WAL sender rate limits
relevant_past_incidents.lesson: High‑write features must be load‑tested for replication impact; enforce WAL sender limits and monitor replica_lag_seconds with 5 s and 15 s thresholds.

investigation_steps: Verify current WAL sender pending bytes via pg_stat_replication
Check replica‑3 I/O metrics (disk queue, throughput)
Confirm replica IOPS allocation
Inspect write_lag and flush_lag values
Review recent batch import throughput and rate
Check if WAL compression is enabled
Ensure replication alerts are configured for 5 s and 15 s thresholds
analysis.recommended_next_action: Throttle the batch import to 500 rows/s, increase replica IOPS to at least 6000, enable WAL compression, and set a WAL sender rate limit. Update monitoring to alert on replica_lag_seconds >5 s and >15 s.
analysis.memory_influence: Recalled memories of incident TEST‑001 directly informed the cause assessment, recommended actions, and lessons applied to this incident.

title: Order history pages loading slowly, stale data from standby database
symptoms: Customers report that order history and account pages are slow and sometimes show outdated orders. Recently placed orders don't appear for several seconds. Read query latency has roughly tripled. Database alerts for the standby node are firing. The primary looks healthy.
metrics:
Standby replay delay: 28s (normally < 1s)
Read query p95 latency: 2.4s (normally 600ms)
Standby CPU: 94%, disk I/O wait: 38%
Primary CPU: 45%, write throughput up ~3x since 14:10 UTC
Error rate: 4% on read endpoints
logs:
WARN  orders-api  read query on standby exceeded 2000ms (p95)
WARN  orders-api  stale read detected: order not found on standby, fell back to primary
ALERT postgres-standby-01: replay delay above threshold (28s)
ERROR orders-api  statement timeout on standby: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1
recent_change: Nightly data backfill job for the orders table was moved to run at 14:00 UTC instead of overnight, generating heavy write volume on the primary.

analysis.summary: The incident involves slow and stale reads from the standby PostgreSQL node after a recent change that increased write traffic on the primary. The standby replay delay has spiked to 28 s, causing read queries to time out or fallback to the primary, leading to high latency and stale data.

likely_causes.cause: Increased write load on primary due to nightly backfill job now running at 14:00 UTC
likely_causes.reasoning: Heavy write volume increases WAL generation, causing the standby to lag behind and exceed its replay delay threshold.

likely_causes.cause: Standby CPU and I/O saturation (CPU 94%, disk I/O wait 38%)
likely_causes.reasoning: High resource utilization on the standby hampers its ability to replay WAL quickly, exacerbating the delay.

likely_causes.cause: Read queries hitting the standby during high latency
likely_causes.reasoning: The application attempts to read from standby, leading to timeouts and fallback to primary, which further increases load.

investigation_steps: Check WAL generation rate on primary during backfill period.
Verify standby replication slots and ensure no lagging slots are causing backlog.
Inspect standby disk I/O and CPU usage; consider adding I/O capacity or moving to faster storage.
Confirm that the application is configured to read from primary when standby lag exceeds a threshold.
Review backfill job to see if it can be partitioned or throttled to reduce peak write load.
Check for any recent configuration changes to PostgreSQL replication settings.
Examine logs for any errors or warnings on both primary and standby around the time of the spike.
analysis.recommended_next_action: Temporarily pause the nightly backfill job or throttle its write rate until the standby can catch up. Configure the application to read from the primary when standby lag exceeds 10 s to avoid stale data and high latency. Monitor replication lag and standby resource usage closely.

title: Dashboard numbers out of date after bulk import, reports timing out
symptoms: Executives report that revenue and signup dashboards show numbers from several minutes ago. Some report queries time out. The issue started shortly after a large customer data import began. The reporting database node is under heavy load and database lag alerts are firing. The main application database is responding normally.
metrics:
Reporting replica replication delay: 41s (normally < 2s)
Report query p95 latency: 6.1s (normally 900ms)
Replica CPU: 97%, disk I/O wait: 45%
Primary write throughput: up ~4x since 09:20 UTC
Dashboard error rate: 6%
logs:
WARN  analytics-dashboard  report query exceeded 5000ms on reporting replica
WARN  analytics-dashboard  data freshness check failed: replica behind primary by 41s
ALERT postgres-reporting-replica: replication delay above threshold (41s)
ERROR analytics-dashboard  statement timeout: SELECT date_trunc('hour', created_at), count(*) FROM signups GROUP BY 1
recent_change: Marketing started a bulk import of 2M customer records at 09:15 UTC during business hours, with no throttling.

analysis.summary: The analytics‑dashboard service is experiencing stale data and query timeouts due to a large bulk import that has overloaded the reporting database replica, causing significant replication lag and high CPU/disk I/O wait.

likely_causes.cause: Replication lag from bulk write load on primary database
likely_causes.reasoning: The reporting replica shows a 41s delay, far above the normal <2s threshold, coinciding with a 4x increase in primary write throughput.

likely_causes.cause: Replica resource exhaustion (CPU 97%, disk I/O wait 45%)
likely_causes.reasoning: High CPU and I/O wait on the replica indicate it cannot keep up with the write stream, leading to query timeouts.
The import started at 09:15 UTC without throttling, likely generating a burst of writes that overwhelmed the replica.

investigation_steps:
Check current replication lag and confirm it is still >30s; if so, consider pausing the bulk import or throttling writes.
Examine the replica’s WAL receiver and archiver logs for errors.
Verify that the replica’s autovacuum and maintenance tasks are running; a backlog could exacerbate lag.
Inspect the primary’s write queue and see if any long‑running transactions are blocking replication.
Check the replica’s disk usage and I/O queue lengths; consider adding SSD or increasing I/O capacity.
Review the bulk import job to see if it can be split into smaller batches or run during off‑peak hours.
Confirm that the application’s read queries are directed to the replica and that failover or read‑through options are available.
Monitor the replica’s CPU and I/O metrics after any changes to ensure they drop below thresholds.
analysis.recommended_next_action: Temporarily pause the bulk import and throttle subsequent writes to the primary. Once replication lag falls below 10s and replica resource usage normalizes, resume the import in smaller batches or during off‑peak hours. Additionally, consider adding a dedicated reporting replica or scaling the existing one to handle peak write loads.

analysis.summary: Orders-service is experiencing order placement timeouts due to database connection pool exhaustion after a flash sale doubled traffic. The pool is at its default size of 80/80 active connections with 61 queued requests, and the database reports 97% of max_connections in use. likely_causes.cause: Connection pool exhaustion caused by increased traffic
likely_causes.reasoning: Logs show "too many clients" and the pool is at 80/80 active. Memory about INC-101 documents identical symptoms when a flash sale doubled traffic and the pool was exhausted.
Alert shows 97% of max_connections used; memory about INC-101 notes DB connections at 99% during a similar incident.

likely_causes.cause: Insufficient pool size for peak traffic
likely_causes.reasoning: Default pool size of 80 was not sized for the doubled order volume; memory about INC-101 recommends sizing pools for peak traffic and alerting when usage exceeds 80%.

relevant_past_incidents.relevance: Connection pool exhaustion caused HTTP 500s and latency spikes in payment-api during a traffic surge.
relevant_past_incidents.previous_resolution: Increased connection pool to 200, restarted pods gradually; errors dropped within 5 minutes.

analysis.recommended_next_action: Increase the orders-service connection pool size to at least 200 (or proportionally to the doubled traffic) and restart the pods gradually to apply the new configuration.
